status: 12 root-approved entries prepared in isolated runtime artifacts; remaining entries are held or unadmitted

entries.title: Hold your claws still
entries.body:
The shrimp wanted to help. He offered to remove something from one of my branches.

I asked which thing.

He pointed with a claw. I could feel the point touching me, so I asked him not to close it while we discussed this.

He said the little pale bits looked untidy. There were so many of them. Perhaps I hadn't noticed.

I opened the nearest polyp.

He drew his claw back. I opened another. He backed into a third. I let that one stay closed until he'd stopped apologizing.

He has offered to bring me something instead. I told him to describe it before putting it down.

image.sceneMatch: Visible shrimp is among the pale polyps with claws extended. Fictional mistaken tidying concerns the actual living structures around him, not unseen prey.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Voyage to the Ridge 2022
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: A shrimp peeks out from the branches of an Iridogorgia coral observed at a depth of 1,680 meters (5,512 feet) during Dive 10 of the second Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition.

entries.title: Come one, come several
entries.body:
I told one crinoid he could stay. Apparently I said it in a very welcoming shape.

There are now crinoids on the branch I use to gesture about the crinoids.

image.sceneMatch: Many feather stars visibly occupy the spiral coral. Gesturing is fictional personification of branch posture, not deliberate coral locomotion.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
This spiral Iridogorgia coral, seen during Dive 19 of the 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones expedition, was covered in crinoids, an unusual observation. Throughout the dive, we observed 29 different species of coral, including corals belonging to the genera Metallogorgia, Paramuricea, Acanella, Paramuricea, Hemicorallium, Acanthogorgia, Clavularia, Anthomastus, Iridogorgia, Paragorgia, Isidella, Swiftia, Candidella, and Chrysogorgia.

Learn more

entries.title: The hungry section
entries.body:
I attempted to think about the whole ocean. A small piece of it brushed one of my mouths, and I ate it.

I am still thinking about the ocean, but that piece was excellent.

image.sceneMatch: Close-up shows numerous open polyps reaching into water. Suspension feeding supplies the interruption, with no visible captured animal claimed.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Deepwater Wonders of Wake
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: A close look at the beautiful central spiral of an octocoral in the genus Iridogorgia, observed during a dive on an unnamed seamount as part of the Deepwater Wonders of Wake: Exploring the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument expedition.

entries.title: A little uneven
entries.body: The new end has grown in a direction I wasn't planning. I've spent so long being beautiful that I resent how much I like this part.

image.sceneMatch: Whole spiral coral shows an irregular upward-growing end; the response is fictional vanity directed at its actual asymmetry.

provenance.creator: Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2022 ROV and Mapping Shakedown.
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: This spiraling coral (Iridogorgia magnispiralis), reaching several meters tall, was seen during Dive 04 of the 2022 ROV and Mapping Shakedown.

entries.title: The little grip
entries.body:
I can tell when he arrives. A small weight on a branch, then another, then the peculiar stop while he decides where to put the rest of his legs.

I used to wait for that stop so I could suggest a better place. There was always a better place. Higher, where the current was stronger. Lower, where he wouldn't pull. He would go where I suggested. I was pleased with how well we understood each other.

Then one day he arrived and did not stop. He climbed straight past the place he used to choose.

I felt proud for a moment. Then I wished he were slower.

Today he has settled on the awkward branch again. I can feel him gripping it. I have thought of three better places and said nothing.

He's taking his time.

image.sceneMatch: Multiple squat lobsters perched on branches; imagined remembered tactile arrival is carried by visible grips. No known species lifespan or long migration claimed.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2012
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
This chrysogorgid octocoral, with its characteristic spiral form, belongs to the genus Iridogorgia. This stunning example was seen in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico during a 2012 expedition. Note the squat lobsters delicately perched atop its branches. Characteristics that can help scientists identify the type of Iridogorgia include the distance between parts of the coil along the main axis and the shape of the polyps.

This image won the Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest for the ‘Exploring the Seafloor’ category as part of our Celebrating Our Ocean Planet campaign.

From: Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest Archive.

entries.title: Long neck, short answer
entries.body:
Someone at the bottom asked what I could see from up here. I said I hadn't got eyes.

He asked why I'd gone to all that trouble.

image.sceneMatch: Long stalk and cup tower over seafloor. Sponge has no eyes; dialogue is fiction. Joke does not grant sponge sight.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2025 Beyond the Blue
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: A large Caulophacus sponge towers more than 2 meters (6.5 feet) off the seafloor. We saw many of these tall sponges along the slope and on the summit flats of the seamount explored during Dive 13 of the Papahānaumokuākea ROV and Mapping expedition.

entries.title: I didn't feel it
entries.body:
He found the little fold before I did. Tucked himself into it with all those legs and announced that it was a fine place.

I said there wasn't a fold there.

He said he was in it.

I tried to account for him. I knew where the water passed, where I held against the current, where something brushed my surface. I couldn't turn any of that into a picture of the place he meant.

He described it again. Patiently this time. There was a narrow opening, a curve, a darker bit. He said it would look obvious if I could see it.

I couldn't. He stayed anyway.

Now when something small moves there, I don't have to know what I look like to know who it is.

image.sceneMatch: Squat lobster actually nestled in a deep fold of the sponge. Narrator lacks visual sense; guest provides exterior account. No new shell or house-moving plot.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2015 Hohonu Moana
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: A squat lobster hides within the crevice of a large stalked glass sponge in the genus Caulophacus. Seen during a dive to explore a sharp ridge that extended west from East Salmon Bank as part of the 2015 Hohonu Moana: Exploring Deep Waters off Hawaii expedition.

entries.title: How we stand
entries.body: The other two lean the same way I do. We have never discussed it. I was beginning to feel understood until the current changed and they both abandoned my position.

image.sceneMatch: Three Caulophacus sponge heads visibly aligned; current-responsive posture is literal. Keep separate from Pip's leadership claim: Oswald seeks agreement, not followers.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Hohonu Moana 2016
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: This glass sponge of the genus Caulophacus was seen while exploring on a ridge extending to the southeast of Castellano Seamount, south of the Midway Islands, as part of the 2016 Hohonu Moana: Exploring Deep Waters off Hawaiʻi expedition. These sponges, which belong to the Class Hexactinellida, get their common name of “glass sponge” because their skeletons are made of silica, which is the same material used to make glass…but glass sponges are not glass, per se.

entries.status: held for lead: current-driven agreement reversal too close to Pip

entries.title: The softer face
entries.body:
I've been keeping my mouth closed when she comes by. It seems to help.

Today she came closer and asked if I was ill.

image.sceneMatch: Pale lizardfish has closed mouth and conspicuous yellow eye. No prey suffering; misunderstanding arises from his effort not to look threatening.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Mountains in the Deep: Exploring the Central Pacific Basin
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
This deep-sea lizardfish (Bathysaurus mollis) was seen on Dive 08 of the Mountains in the Deep: Exploring the Central Pacific Basin expedition. Bathysaurus have beautiful, yellow eyes and a mouth full of impressive teeth. They are apex predators in the abyss and are known to strike at other large fishes. These lizardfish are widely observed on abyssal plains. Scientists were able to identify this one down to species (Bathysaurus mollis) due to its pale coloration.

From: A Dive Into the Abyss.

entries.title: A proper apology
entries.body:
I frightened him. I didn't mean to, which I kept trying to explain while he got farther away.

The farther away he went, the wider I opened my mouth to make myself clear.

Eventually I noticed the difficulty.

I stayed on the bottom and let him put a comfortable amount of ocean between us. There was plenty. I had no objection to his using it.

When he stopped, I closed my mouth.

We sat like that for a while. I wanted to say I was sorry. I wanted him to know I had noticed. But every version of that involved opening my mouth again.

He moved a little closer before leaving. I have decided to count that.

image.sceneMatch: Close-up of pale lizardfish's many exposed teeth supports frightening appearance and failed reassurance. Stranger is fictional, no predation portrayed.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2025 Beyond the Blue
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: A close look at the impressive teeth on a deep-sea lizardfish (Bathysauridae) encountered during Dive 02 of the Papahānaumokuākea ROV and Mapping expedition at a depth of 4,855 meters (15,928 feet).

entries.title: Resting opinion
entries.body: I was enjoying myself. Someone came over to ask what was wrong, so now there is an answer.

image.sceneMatch: Front-facing sea toad's downturned mouth and resting body carry the discrepancy between expression and private enjoyment.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2025 Beyond the Blue
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: While we saw few fish during Dive 10 of the Papahānaumokuākea ROV and Mapping expedition, we were lucky enough to catch a glimpse of this sea toad (Chaunacops sp.).

entries.title: Red all over
entries.body: She said she liked a little color. I may have overdone the rest of me.

image.sceneMatch: Brilliant red sea toad fills the frame. Natural pigment, not a claim of voluntary instantaneous color change. Light innuendo or vanity, not documented courtship display.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Deep-Sea Symphony: Exploring the Musicians Seamounts
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
On September 8, 2017, during the Deep-Sea Symphony: Exploring the Musicians Seamounts expedition, this bright-red sea toad or coffinfish (Chaunacops species) was seen at a depth of 3,148 meters (1.96 miles) during a remotely operated vehicle dive at a seamount ridge dubbed “Beach Ridge” in the Musicians Seamount group northeast of Oʼahu, Hawaiian Islands. The fish’s identity is a mystery.

From: The Mysterious Identity of the Bright-Red Sea Toad.

entries.title: Something light
entries.body:
I said I'd only had a little mud. He looked through me.

I wish that phrase were less exact.

image.sceneMatch: Transparent Enypniastes shows its internal sediment-filled intestine. Literal transparency makes her understatement untenable.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Exploring Deep-sea Habitats off Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
The swimming sea cucumber, Enypniastes eximia, sometimes referred to as the “headless chicken monster,” is a widespread species present in the abyss. It is encountered widely around the world with records from the Gulf of Mexico, Tropical Atlantic, East Atlantic, New Zealand, and the Southern Ocean (Antarctica). This one was seen off Puerto Rico in 2018.

Swimming sea cucumbers have a special ‘flap’ which they use to ‘lift’ themselves off the seafloor. The transparent body reveals the sediment-filled intestine looping around from the mouth (top) to the anus (bottom).

From: Holothurian Hill.

entries.title: The view from dinner
entries.body:
I left the bottom because I wanted to do something that wasn't eating mud.

Up I went. The flap caught the water. The ground moved away, which was an excellent start. I let myself rise until there was room beneath me, room I wasn't about to put in my mouth.

For a while I felt wonderfully unlike myself.

Then I felt the weight of dinner inside me. A little piece of the place I'd left, coming along. I had carried it up here without asking whether it wanted a better view.

Somebody else had been feeding beside me before I rose. She was probably still there, working through the soft patch I had found.

I hoped she would wonder where I'd gone. Then I remembered the patch.

I may have left too soon.

image.sceneMatch: Enypniastes suspended above bottom with conspicuous intestine. Flight and carried sediment are literal; philosophical adventure collapses into remembered appetite rather than an appended moral.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
This image won the Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest for the ‘Exploring the Deep Ocean World and Its Biodiversity’ category as part of our Celebrating Our Ocean Planet campaign. Common names for this bizarre sea cucumber (Enypniastes eximia) seen during the Gulf of Mexico 2017 expedition include Spanish dancer and headless chicken monster. These animals spend most of their time on the seafloor, feeding off surface sediments, but they can swim if they want to get somewhere more quickly or to evade a predator.

From: Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest Archive.

entries.status: held for lead: carried-dinner mechanism resembles existing unillustrated Vera Veil arc

entries.title: A small adjustment
entries.body: I've spent so long waiting for something to come past that moving six inches feels like abandoning my principles. The new view contains a rock. I am excited about the rock.

image.sceneMatch: Full body lies along open sediment near a dark rock. Six-inch move and private excitement are imagined, with the visible rock central rather than unseen prey.

provenance.creator: NOAA/MBARI
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: Bathysaur or highfin lizardfish (Bathysaurus mollis) at the Davidson Seamount (2375 meters depth). This is one of three Pacific coast species. This fish is often found very still on the bottom; lying-in-wait as an ambush predator on unsuspecting prey items.

entries.title: You missed a bit
entries.body:
The lobster described my outside to me again. He was doing very well until he said I looked clean.

I've got him to start over and include the holes.

image.sceneMatch: White sponge exterior has many clear pores, essential to Oswald's demand for an account that does not erase how his body works. Guest is remembered, not claimed pictured.

provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:

entries.title: Passing through
entries.body:
I took one step and stopped. There was a better place for the other fin, but getting it there required admitting the first step had been poorly chosen.

A fish went past. Then back. He asked whether I needed help.

I said I was looking at something.

He settled beside me to see it too. We stayed there for a while, both looking at a patch of bare rock. Every so often he edged closer. I thought he might be about to leave, but he was only trying to work out what he'd missed.

Eventually I took the second step.

He gasped. I have no idea what he thinks happened.

image.sceneMatch: Sea toad's walking fins are planted on uneven pale rock, with body poised above them. Remembered awkward movement and companion are fictional; no claim of a photographed struggle.

entries.title: Answer the question
entries.body: It's difficult to maintain a private appetite when everyone can see the last one. I've begun asking the fish what they've eaten. They change the subject remarkably fast.

image.sceneMatch: Transparent body exposes the intestine. The fictional social confrontation concerns this visible lack of privacy, not an attempt to hide the gut by turning sideways.

provenance.creator: NOAA Okeanos Explorer
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: A spectacular image of a benthopelagic sea cucumber swimming in the near freezing waters of the abyss.Image captured by the Little Hercules ROV at 3205 meters depth on "Site K," explored July 27, 2010 during the INDEX SATAL 2010 Expedition. Image courtesy of NOAA Okeanos Explorer Program, INDEX-SATAL 2010.

entries.title: The evidence inside
entries.body:
A fish asked what I believed in. I began quite well, I thought. He interrupted to ask about the loop of mud.

I told him that was a separate argument. He said it seemed to be the one I was carrying.

image.sceneMatch: Whole suspended body displays its looped sediment-filled intestine. Philosophical vanity meets plainly visible appetite.

provenance.creator: NOAA Okeanos Explorer
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: Enypniastes eximia observed in the abyss off Puerto Rico by the NOAA Okeanos Explorer mission.

entries.status: held: exact image already bound to Vera Veil in runtime; do not admit

entries.title: The unhelpful close-up
entries.body:
She said I had lovely arms. I spread them a little so she could admire the arrangement.

My mouth was right in the middle. I was chewing. There was nowhere else to put it.

image.sceneMatch: Close-up shows arms radiating around the mouth; no alternative facial pose possible. Fictional flirtation arises from this actual bodily arrangement.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
A close look at a yellow stalked crinoid. All crinoids are suspension feeders, subsisting on the smorgasbord of small plankton and detritus that drift past their outstretched arms. Most crinoids array their arms in a bowl or dish shape with the arm tips flexed back into the current and the top of the stalk bent so that the central mouth, visible in this image, faces away from the current. In addition to yellow crinoids, we also saw red and white (both stalked and unstalked) crinoids during Dive 06 of the 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones expedition.

Learn more

entries.title: One bright place
entries.body:
A little one grew below us. At first I mistook the thin pale line for something caught on the rock. Then there were arms.

He kept them so close together that I wanted to explain how much water he was missing. I had an explanation ready. It involved opening out, being less afraid, several things that are easy to say when you already reach over the rock.

Then a small current found the hollow where he was. His arms opened into it.

He ate before I did.

I felt pleased for him. There was something else in there too. I will not be discussing that with the little one.

image.sceneMatch: Field of yellow stalked crinoids includes small individuals lower on rough lava beside taller ones. Fictional growth and feeding competition use visible size and topographic differences. No parentage claimed.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
Pillow lava formations with sediment ponds were abundant on Dive 06 of the 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones expedition, and they were often covered in fields of stalked crinoids, as shown in this scene from a depth of 2,126 meters (6,975 feet).

Learn more

entries.title: Worth the stretch
entries.body:
A grain touched the tip of an arm. I brought it all the way in. It was a grain. I tried the next one anyway. It was food.

Nobody saw either of these enormous events.

image.sceneMatch: Open arms against particle-filled water support tiny feeding encounters. Comic scale belongs to a suspension feeder, with no suffering or false grasping anatomy.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
We saw both stalked and unstalked crinoids during Dive 11 of the 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration. The sea lily shown here is a stalked crinoid.

Learn more

entries.title: Almost a circle
entries.body:
Someone said I had come full circle. I asked him to follow the branch and check.

He's still going. It was an unkind way to make a point, but he started it.

image.sceneMatch: Top-down spiral makes almost-circular mistaken geometry immediate. Fictional small guest traverses actual spiral rather than a closed ring.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2025 Beyond the Blue
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: This beautifully spiraling Iridogorgia coral was observed at a depth of 1,695 meters (5,561 feet) during Papahānaumokuākea ROV and Mapping expedition Dive 01. Iridogorgia, along with Paragorgia, Metallogorgia, and Paramercidae, were the dominant coral fauna present during the dive.

entries.title: The upper end
entries.body:
There is a part of me that wasn't here when the shrimp first arrived.

He climbed past it today without stopping. It bothered me. I had grown it through a great deal of unremarkable water. There had been lean days. There had been little catches that didn't seem worth mentioning. Somehow they had become this.

I asked if he noticed anything different.

He turned around. Examined the nearest branch. Moved a few legs. I began to regret the question.

Then he climbed onto the new bit and stayed there.

I had wanted him to say something. His weight was better.

image.sceneMatch: Whole coral shows pale growing branches above a long stalk. Arrival and touch are fictional remembered interactions; growth is not claimed to occur within the photographed instant.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Discovering the Deep: Exploring Remote Pacific MPAs
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: The beautiful curly-cue shape shown here is a characteristic of this chrysogorgid octocoral, called Iridogorgia. We imaged this one while exploring on an unnamed seamount west of Winslow Reef complex, within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone, as part of the Discovering the Deep: Exploring Remote Pacific Marine Protected Areas expedition.
